    <div class="content">
        <h2 id="overview"><i class="fas fa-network-wired"></i> 1. What is Third-Party Risk Management?</h2>

        <h3>Understanding the Basics</h3>
        <p>Imagine you have the most secure house in the neighborhood - alarm systems, cameras, reinforced doors.
            But you give your house key to a cleaning service, and they get robbed. Now criminals have your key.</p>

        <p>This is <strong>third-party risk</strong> in a nutshell. Your organization might have excellent security,
            but you share data and access with vendors who might not. When THEY get breached, YOU suffer the
            consequences.</p>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Think of it like this:</strong> Every vendor with access to
            your data or systems is a potential door into your organization. TPRM is about knowing which doors you
            have, who holds the keys, and making sure they're locked properly.
        </div>

        <h3>Real-World Supply Chain Attacks (Learn from Others)</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Year</th>
                    <th>Incident</th>
                    <th>What Happened</th>
                    <th>Impact</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>2020</td>
                    <td>SolarWinds</td>
                    <td>Attackers compromised SolarWinds' build system, inserted malware into software updates</td>
                    <td>18,000+ organizations downloaded compromised updates, including US government agencies</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>2023</td>
                    <td>MOVEit Transfer</td>
                    <td>Zero-day in file transfer software exploited before patch available</td>
                    <td>2,500+ organizations breached, 65M+ individuals affected</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>2023</td>
                    <td>Okta via Rightway</td>
                    <td>Third-party healthcare admin vendor breached, exposing Okta employee data</td>
                    <td>5,000 Okta employees' personal info exposed via support vendor</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>2024</td>
                    <td>Change Healthcare</td>
                    <td>Healthcare claims processor ransomed, affecting entire US healthcare system</td>
                    <td>Millions of patients' data exposed, billions in damages</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> The SolarWinds Lesson:</strong> Organizations with
            multi-million dollar security budgets were compromised because their network monitoring vendor was
            hacked. The attackers didn't need to break through firewalls—they walked in through a trusted software
            update. This is why vendor security matters as much as your own.
        </div>

        <h3>The Technical Definition</h3>
        <p><strong>Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM)</strong> is the process of identifying, assessing, and
            mitigating risks that arise from organizations you do business with—vendors, suppliers, partners,
            contractors, and service providers.</p>

        <p>Third parties often have access to your systems, data, or networks, creating potential pathways for data
            breaches, operational disruptions, compliance violations, and reputational damage.</p>

        <h3>Types of Third-Party Risks</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Risk Category</th>
                    <th>Description</th>
                    <th>Real Example</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Cybersecurity</strong></td>
                    <td>Security vulnerabilities and breaches at vendors</td>
                    <td>SolarWinds: Malicious code in software update compromised 18,000+ customers</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Operational</strong></td>
                    <td>Vendor failures affecting your operations</td>
                    <td>AWS outage 2021: Thousands of websites and services went offline for hours</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Compliance</strong></td>
                    <td>Vendor violations affecting your compliance</td>
                    <td>You're still liable if your cloud provider mishandles GDPR-protected data</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Strategic</strong></td>
                    <td>Changes affecting business relationship</td>
                    <td>VMware acquired by Broadcom; major licensing and pricing changes</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Reputational</strong></td>
                    <td>Vendor actions damaging your brand</td>
                    <td>Customers blame you for breaches, even if the vendor was at fault</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Fourth-Party</strong></td>
                    <td>Risks from your vendor's vendors</td>
                    <td>Your SaaS provider uses AWS, which uses third-party datacenters...</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Key Insight:</strong> You can outsource the work, but you
            can't outsource the responsibility. Regulators and customers hold YOU accountable when your vendor
            fails, regardless of whose fault it technically was.
        </div>

        <h2 id="program"><i class="fas fa-building"></i> 2. Building a TPRM Program</h2>
        <h3>Program Components</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Governance:</strong> Policies, roles, and executive oversight</li>
            <li><strong>Inventory:</strong> Complete register of all third parties</li>
            <li><strong>Risk Assessment:</strong> Methodology for evaluating vendor risk</li>
            <li><strong>Due Diligence:</strong> Pre-contract security evaluation</li>
            <li><strong>Contracts:</strong> Security requirements in agreements</li>
            <li><strong>Monitoring:</strong> Ongoing oversight of vendor security</li>
            <li><strong>Incident Response:</strong> Plans for vendor-related incidents</li>
            <li><strong>Exit Planning:</strong> Strategies for terminating relationships</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="tiering"><i class="fas fa-layer-group"></i> 3. Vendor Risk Tiering</h2>
        <p>Not all vendors require the same level of scrutiny. Tier vendors based on risk factors:</p>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Tier</th>
                    <th>Criteria</th>
                    <th>Assessment Level</th>
                    <th>Review Frequency</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td style="color: var(--accent-red);"><strong>Critical</strong></td>
                    <td>Access to sensitive data, critical operations, single source</td>
                    <td>Comprehensive assessment, on-site audit</td>
                    <td>Annual</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td style="color: #f59e0b;"><strong>High</strong></td>
                    <td>PII access, significant operations impact</td>
                    <td>Detailed questionnaire, evidence review</td>
                    <td>Annual</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td style="color: var(--accent-cyan);"><strong>Medium</strong></td>
                    <td>Internal data access, moderate impact</td>
                    <td>Standard questionnaire</td>
                    <td>Every 2 years</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td style="color: var(--accent-green);"><strong>Low</strong></td>
                    <td>Public info only, minimal impact</td>
                    <td>Simplified assessment</td>
                    <td>Every 3 years</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>Tiering Factors</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Type and sensitivity of data accessed</li>
            <li>Criticality to business operations</li>
            <li>Network connectivity and access level</li>
            <li>Regulatory requirements</li>
            <li>Substitutability (can you switch vendors easily?)</li>
            <li>Geographic and jurisdictional considerations</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="assessment"><i class="fas fa-clipboard-check"></i> 4. Security Assessment Methods</h2>

        <h3>Assessment Techniques</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Security Questionnaires:</strong> SIG, CAIQ, or custom questionnaires covering security
                controls</li>
            <li><strong>Certifications Review:</strong> SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS compliance reports</li>
            <li><strong>Penetration Test Results:</strong> Request recent pen test summaries</li>
            <li><strong>On-Site Audits:</strong> Physical inspection for critical vendors</li>
            <li><strong>Continuous Monitoring:</strong> Security ratings services (BitSight, SecurityScorecard)</li>
            <li><strong>Financial Review:</strong> Assess financial stability and viability</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Pro Tip:</strong> A SOC 2 Type II report is the gold standard
            for SaaS vendors. It provides independent assurance of security controls over a period of time
            (typically 6-12 months).
        </div>

        <h3>Key Assessment Areas</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Information security policies and governance</li>
            <li>Access control and identity management</li>
            <li>Data protection and encryption</li>
            <li>Network security and segmentation</li>
            <li>Vulnerability management and patching</li>
            <li>Incident response capabilities</li>
            <li>Business continuity and disaster recovery</li>
            <li>Employee security training</li>
            <li>Subcontractor/fourth-party management</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="contracts"><i class="fas fa-file-contract"></i> 5. Contractual Requirements</h2>
        <p>Every vendor contract handling sensitive data should include:</p>

        <h3>Essential Contract Clauses</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Security Requirements:</strong> Minimum security controls required</li>
            <li><strong>Data Handling:</strong> How data can be used, stored, and transmitted</li>
            <li><strong>Audit Rights:</strong> Your right to audit or request security evidence</li>
            <li><strong>Breach Notification:</strong> Timeline and process for notifying you of incidents (≤24-72
                hours)</li>
            <li><strong>Subcontracting:</strong> Approval requirements for subcontractors</li>
            <li><strong>Data Return/Destruction:</strong> Obligations at contract end</li>
            <li><strong>Liability & Indemnification:</strong> Financial responsibility for breaches</li>
            <li><strong>Insurance:</strong> Minimum cyber insurance coverage</li>
            <li><strong>Compliance:</strong> Obligation to maintain regulatory compliance</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="monitoring"><i class="fas fa-eye"></i> 6. Ongoing Monitoring</h2>
        <h3>Continuous Monitoring Methods</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Security Ratings:</strong> Subscribe to services that continuously monitor vendor security
                posture</li>
            <li><strong>News Monitoring:</strong> Track vendor-related security news and breaches</li>
            <li><strong>Periodic Reassessment:</strong> Regular questionnaire updates based on tier</li>
            <li><strong>Compliance Verification:</strong> Request updated certifications annually</li>
            <li><strong>Performance Metrics:</strong> Track SLAs, uptime, and incident history</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Red Flags to Watch</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Declining security ratings</li>
            <li>Reported data breaches or incidents</li>
            <li>Key security personnel departures</li>
            <li>Acquisition or merger activity</li>
            <li>Financial distress indicators</li>
            <li>Failure to renew certifications</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="incidents"><i class="fas fa-bell"></i> 7. Third-Party Incident Response</h2>
        <p>When a vendor experiences a security incident:</p>

        <h3>Immediate Actions</h3>
        <ol>
            <li>Assess if your data was affected</li>
            <li>Activate your incident response team</li>
            <li>Document all communications</li>
            <li>Determine regulatory notification requirements</li>
            <li>Communicate with affected stakeholders</li>
            <li>Consider temporary access restrictions</li>
        </ol>

        <h3>Post-Incident</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Request root cause analysis from vendor</li>
            <li>Verify remediation steps taken</li>
            <li>Conduct lessons learned review</li>
            <li>Consider relationship continuation or exit</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="exit"><i class="fas fa-door-open"></i> 8. Exit Strategies</h2>
        <p>Plan for vendor transitions before you need them:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Document data formats and migration procedures</li>
            <li>Identify alternative vendors in advance</li>
            <li>Ensure contractual right to data export</li>
            <li>Plan for service continuity during transition</li>
            <li>Verify data destruction after transition</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="checklist"><i class="fas fa-tasks"></i> 9. TPRM Checklist</h2>
        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> TPRM Implementation Checklist:</strong>
            <ul style="margin-top: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 0;">
                <li>Create a complete vendor inventory</li>
                <li>Establish vendor tiering methodology</li>
                <li>Define assessment questionnaires for each tier</li>
                <li>Create contract security addendum template</li>
                <li>Implement vendor security rating monitoring</li>
                <li>Document third-party incident response procedures</li>
                <li>Develop exit strategy templates</li>
                <li>Assign TPRM ownership and governance</li>
                <li>Train procurement and legal teams</li>
                <li>Establish periodic review cadence</li>
            </ul>
        </div>
